plant.name: Plant Cell
plant.clinicalContext: A useful non-human baseline for teaching why cell walls and chloroplasts are absent from patient tissue samples.

occurrence.title: Leaves, stems, roots
occurrence.body: Plant cells form tissues that store energy, move water, and turn sunlight into sugars.

nucleus.name: Nucleus
nucleus.subtitle: The control center
nucleus.note: The nucleus is surrounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope, which contains pores that regulate molecular traffic.
nucleus.fact: The nucleus was one of the first cell structures discovered.

chloroplast.name: Chloroplast
chloroplast.subtitle: The light harvester
chloroplast.note: Chloroplasts convert light energy into chemical energy and give many plant tissues their green color.
chloroplast.fact: A single leaf cell can contain dozens of chloroplasts.

vacuole.name: Vacuole
vacuole.subtitle: The pressure reservoir
vacuole.note: The central vacuole stores water, ions, and small molecules while helping the plant cell remain firm.
vacuole.fact: Vacuoles can occupy most of a mature plant cell.

cellWall.name: Cell Wall
cellWall.subtitle: The rigid frame
cellWall.note: The cell wall gives plant cells their regular shape and protects the membrane beneath it.
cellWall.fact: Cell walls help plants stand upright without a skeleton.

whiteBlood.name: White Blood Cell
whiteBlood.clinicalContext: Immune cell morphology is a bridge from basic cell biology to how clinicians interpret infection, inflammation, and blood smears.

occurrence.title: Blood, lymph, tissues
occurrence.body: White blood cells move through blood and tissue spaces to identify threats and coordinate immune defense.

lysosome.name: Lysosome
lysosome.subtitle: The cleanup vesicle
lysosome.note: Lysosomes help immune cells digest engulfed material and recycle worn cellular components.
lysosome.fact: White blood cells rely heavily on vesicles for defense.

nucleus.name: Lobed Nucleus
nucleus.subtitle: Flexible genome vault
nucleus.note: Many white blood cells have a lobed nucleus that helps them squeeze through tight spaces.
nucleus.fact: Nuclear shape is one clue used to identify immune cell types.

granules.name: Granules
granules.subtitle: The chemical packets
granules.note: Granules store molecules that help immune cells respond quickly to infection or inflammation.
granules.fact: Some immune cells are named by how their granules stain.

neuron.name: Neuron
neuron.clinicalContext: Neuron shape helps learners connect cell structure with bedside neuroanatomy, reflexes, sensation, and motor signaling.

occurrence.title: Brain, spinal cord, nerves
occurrence.body: Neurons carry electrical and chemical signals through long branching networks.

axon.name: Axon
axon.subtitle: The signal highway
axon.note: Some axons in the human body run from the spine to the foot, making neurons among the longest cells in nature.
axon.fact: A nerve impulse can travel at over 100 metres per second.

soma.name: Soma
soma.subtitle: The cell body
soma.note: The soma maintains the neuron and integrates signals arriving from branching dendrites.
soma.fact: Most neuron proteins are made in or near the soma.

dendrites.name: Dendrites
dendrites.subtitle: The receiving branches
dendrites.note: Dendrites increase the surface area available for receiving signals from other cells.
dendrites.fact: A single neuron can receive thousands of synaptic inputs.

epithelial.name: Epithelial Cell
epithelial.clinicalContext: Epithelial polarity and tight junctions make this cell type central to barriers, absorption, and pathology slide interpretation.

occurrence.title: Skin, intestine, airways
occurrence.body: Epithelial cells form protective sheets and absorption surfaces across the body.

microvilli.name: Microvilli
microvilli.subtitle: The absorption brush
microvilli.note: Microvilli increase surface area for absorption and secretion along epithelial sheets.
microvilli.fact: Intestinal microvilli form a dense brush border.

junctions.name: Tight Junctions
junctions.subtitle: The sealed seams
junctions.note: Tight junctions link neighboring epithelial cells and control what passes between them.
junctions.fact: Epithelial barriers are essential for organ boundaries.

nucleus.name: Nucleus
nucleus.subtitle: The instruction store
nucleus.note: The epithelial nucleus stores genetic information and changes position depending on tissue shape.
nucleus.fact: Nuclear shape helps pathologists read tissue samples.

bacteria.name: Bacteria Cell
bacteria.clinicalContext: Cell wall structure provides a clinically relevant path from microscopy and Gram staining to antimicrobial mechanism discussions.

occurrence.title: Soil, water, gut, skin
occurrence.body: Bacteria live in nearly every environment and can exist as independent single cells.

nucleoid.name: Nucleoid
nucleoid.subtitle: The naked genome
nucleoid.note: Unlike eukaryotic cells, bacteria have no nuclear envelope. Their DNA floats in a cytoplasm region called the nucleoid.
nucleoid.fact: There are more bacterial cells in your body than many people expect.

cellWall.name: Cell Wall
cellWall.subtitle: The protective shell
cellWall.note: The bacterial cell wall helps cells resist pressure and gives many species their characteristic shapes.
cellWall.fact: Gram staining reveals differences in bacterial wall structure.

flagellum.name: Flagellum
flagellum.subtitle: The swimming tail
flagellum.note: Some bacteria rotate flagella like tiny motors to move through liquid environments.
flagellum.fact: Bacterial flagella are powered by ion gradients.

animal.name: Animal Cell
animal.clinicalContext: This general eukaryotic model helps learners anchor organelle functions before applying them to human tissues and disease mechanisms.

occurrence.title: Animal tissues
occurrence.body: Animal cells form flexible tissues with membranes, internal organelles, and specialized signaling structures.

mitochondrion.name: Mitochondrion
mitochondrion.subtitle: The energy converter
mitochondrion.note: Mitochondria convert fuel molecules into usable cellular energy through folded inner membranes.
mitochondrion.fact: Mitochondria contain their own small DNA genome.

nucleus.name: Nucleus
nucleus.subtitle: The command room
nucleus.note: The nucleus stores chromosomes and regulates which genes are active in a cell.
nucleus.fact: Not all animal cells keep a nucleus. Mature red blood cells lose theirs.

golgi.name: Golgi Apparatus
golgi.subtitle: The packaging stack
golgi.note: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and ships proteins and lipids to their destinations.
golgi.fact: Secretory cells often have a prominent Golgi apparatus.

muscle.name: Muscle Cell
muscle.clinicalContext: Muscle fiber architecture links microscopic structure with contraction, fatigue, rehabilitation, and neuromuscular disease teaching.

occurrence.title: Skeletal muscles
occurrence.body: Muscle fibers contain repeating contractile bundles that shorten to generate force.

myofibril.name: Myofibril
myofibril.subtitle: The contracting thread
myofibril.note: Each muscle fiber contains hundreds to thousands of myofibrils running its full length, packed tightly together.
myofibril.fact: A single muscle fiber can be up to 30 cm long.

sarcolemma.name: Sarcolemma
sarcolemma.subtitle: The excitable membrane
sarcolemma.note: The sarcolemma conducts electrical signals that trigger contraction throughout the muscle fiber.
sarcolemma.fact: Membrane signals reach deep into fibers through T tubules.

mitochondria.name: Mitochondria
mitochondria.subtitle: The endurance supply
mitochondria.note: Muscle cells need many mitochondria because contraction consumes large amounts of ATP.
mitochondria.fact: Endurance training can increase mitochondrial density.
